cards.title: ECO and the Afghan dilemma
cards.author: editorial
cards.why: This touches upon regional security, Pakistan's foreign policy, and the stability of the Afghanistan-Pakistan border.
cards.summary: Pakistan is facing increased security challenges due to the presence of terror networks in Afghanistan. The Taliban government's refusal to curb these groups undermines regional stability and economic integration. Pakistan is calling for international pressure to hold Kabul accountable for its security commitments.
key_facts: The 30th meeting of the ECO Council of Ministers was held in Islamabad.
Pakistan has expressed serious reservations over the Taliban regime's failure to dismantle terror networks like the TTP.
The 10-member Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) has recently reprimanded Kabul for failing to act as a responsible state.
Stable regional relations are defined by trust rather than just connectivity infrastructure.

vocab.meaning: a state of incompatibility or disagreement

text: Pakistan has once again flagged its rightful concerns pertaining to security fissures emanating from across its western frontier. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar reminded the 30th meeting of the ECO Council of Ministers in Islamabad that the Taliban regime has consistently failed to uphold its promises regarding the eradication of terror networks holed up inside Afghanistan. The non-seriousness of the reclusive administration can be gauged from the fact that no representative participated in the moot, confirming its defiance and contempt for regional concerns on such a vital issue. Kabul has been evading Islamabad's worries by openly pampering a host of non-state actors, including the outlawed TTP, out of political exigency. This has led to a sharp spike in terror activities inside Pakistan. Thus, Dar was spot on when he said no regional state is immune from this backlash and that it is incumbent upon Kabul to act before it is too late. The deputy PM told the regional foreign ministers that a stable Afghanistan is essential for realising geo-economic goals. Likewise, he had a point when he noted that regional integration is not merely about routes and connectivity, but about the trust that defines relationships among sovereign states. This is where Afghanistan is acting like a pariah state, drawing serious reservations from the international community over its conduct and credibility. The 10-member SCO recently reprimanded Kabul, reminding it that it is failing to act as a responsible state in upholding international law and bilateral commitments. Similarly, the UN and other rights bodies have time and again released dossiers detailing the terror networks simmering inside Afghanistan. It goes without saying that a peaceful Afghanistan would be a blessing for regional development and tranquility. The ECO has lagged behind in making meaningful strides over previous decades owing to a lack of consistency in regional collaboration, and it is now held back by the spectre of terrorism. It is time for regional stakeholders to put their heads together and ensure that Afghanistan is persuaded to change course before it slides further into an abyss of instability.

cards.title: Unchecked abuse
cards.author: editorial
cards.why: It highlights critical failures in governance, child protection, and human rights implementation within the Pakistani context.
cards.summary: Domestic worker abuse in Pakistan is fueled by poverty and a lack of effective regulatory oversight. Vulnerable children are often employed in private households, leaving them isolated and exposed to exploitation. Despite existing legislation, enforcement is weak and child labour remains a severe violation of rights.
key_facts: The Islamabad Capital Territory Domestic Workers Act, 2022, prohibits the employment of children below 16 years of age.
Domestic employment is currently one of the least regulated labour sectors in Pakistan.
Systemic poverty forces many families to send children into domestic service, hindering their education and social mobility.
Accountability for domestic abuse often fails because workers lack accessible complaint mechanisms.
text: Abuse of domestic workers in Pakistan persists largely because those subjected to it have few means of seeking protection or justice. Poverty compels thousands of families to send their children into domestic employment, often without any assurance of their safety or wellbeing. Within private households, these children remain entirely dependent on their employers, with little opportunity to report mistreatment or escape abusive conditions. The absence of effective oversight has allowed exploitation to continue despite laws intended to protect vulnerable workers. The death of 13-year-old Fatima, who was employed at the Islamabad residence of a senior government officer, raises questions about the protection afforded to children working in private homes. Preliminary medical findings reportedly revealed marks of physical violence on her body, while allegations that local police initially attempted to suppress the matter require investigation. The circumstances of her death must be established and those responsible, if found guilty, held accountable irrespective of their official position or social standing. Domestic employment remains one of the least regulated forms of labour in Pakistan. Workers frequently lack access to complaint mechanisms. Children face additional risks because they are less able to resist exploitation or recognise violations of their rights. Their employment also deprives them of education and opportunities for social mobility, perpetuating the very poverty that forces them into work. Legislation alone cannot address these conditions. Although the Islamabad Capital Territory Domestic Workers Act, 2022, prohibits the employment of children below 16, enforcement remains inadequate. Provincial governments must ensure that existing labour protections are implemented and that violations are investigated without interference. Effective complaint mechanisms and stronger child protection services are essential to help protect this vulnerable workforce. We, as a society, must realise that domestic workers are entitled to the same dignity and legal protection as other workers.

cards.title: Hidden gender gap in school leadership
cards.author: Jazib Mumtaz
cards.why: It addresses gender studies and governance issues related to institutional equality and educational reform.
cards.summary: Women in Pakistan's public education system face a significant 'leadership gap' despite their high numbers as teachers. Systemic institutional biases and a lack of gender-disaggregated data prevent them from reaching principal and administrative roles. Policy discourse must address these structural barriers to achieve gender equality in school management.
key_facts: In Punjab, less than 1% of female teachers are promoted to principal or vice-principal positions.
The Provincial Annual School Census 2023–24 highlights severe under-representation of women in leadership.
Lack of gender-disaggregated data restricts evidence-based policy making for female career progression.
Structural barriers include workplace harassment, institutional bias, and lack of awareness regarding promotion criteria.
text: There are significant disparities in women's representation in leadership positions within Pakistan's public school education system, reflecting pronounced gender inequalities across provinces. According to the Provincial Annual School Census 202324, the representation of female teachers in principal and vice-principal positions remains extremely low. In Punjab, for instance, less than 1% of female teachers have been promoted to these leadership positions. Similar gender disparities persist in Sindh, Balochistan and Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa. Despite the magnitude of this issue, gender-based inequalities in educational leadership remain largely under-researched and inadequately addressed in policy discourse. A major contributing factor is the lack of comprehensive gender-disaggregated data on professional training, recruitment, promotions, career progression, retention, workplace harassment and women's representation in leadership positions. This data gap limits the ability of policymakers to identify systemic barriers, formulate evidence-based interventions and allocate resources effectively to promote gender equality across the education system. A review of existing education policies also highlights significant institutional and policy gaps. There is an absence of systematic mechanisms to assess structural barriers, including gender-based discrimination and institutional biases, that constrain women's career advancement. Furthermore, limited awareness and understanding of recruitment and promotion procedures, inadequate workplace protection mechanisms against harassment, and the absence of reliable gender-disaggregated leadership data further undermine women's professional progression. Addressing these challenges requires a comprehensive review of existing policies and institutional practices, alongside robust data collection, transparent career advancement procedures, effective workplace protection mechanisms and targeted policy interventions. Women's presence in school leadership enhances instructional quality, builds community trust and increases girls' access to education. Women leaders are linked to safer school settings, stronger teacher support systems and higher learning results, especially for girls, according to data from UNICEF's global analysis 2022. Research from South Asia also demonstrates that gender-responsive leadership improves school administration and aids in removing sociocultural barriers that disproportionately impact female teachers and students. According to UNESCO's 2019 report on educational governance in Pakistan, leadership disparities are closely linked to systemic HR bottlenecks, ambiguous promotion pathways and gender-blind policy frameworks that ignore structural disadvantages faced by women. These findings suggest a positive relationship between women's participation in educational leadership and improved learning outcomes in basic education. Although the National Education Policy Development Framework 2024 acknowledges systemic injustices throughout the educational system, it does not specifically address gender disparities in educational leadership. The framework highlights governance shortcomings, teacher shortages and inadequate implementation mechanisms, but it does not examine how these problems disproportionately impact women. For instance, section 12 of the policy emphasises the need for better management structures and governance issues, but it ignores the gendered hurdles that keep women out of these positions. This omission highlights a significant policy gap. The framework does not incorporate gendered indicators into monitoring frameworks, does not acknowledge the significance of women in decision-making roles for attaining equity, and does not offer measures for developing gender-responsive HR systems. In order to ensure that governance improvements benefit men and women equally and promote better educational outcomes for all children, it is imperative that these discrepancies be addressed. Understanding how gender-based barriers at the policy, administrative and community levels influence school performance and educational equity requires a closer examination of women's leadership within Pakistan's institutional, social and cultural context.

cards.title: Enhancing exports to China
cards.author: Adeel Munawar
cards.why: It provides insight into Pakistan's economic strategy and trade relationship with its largest strategic partner.
cards.summary: Pakistan has significant potential to increase its exports to China by shifting from raw commodities to value-added products. Sectors such as agriculture, food processing, minerals, and textiles remain underdeveloped in the Chinese market. A targeted strategy focusing on branding and direct access to Chinese buyers is essential for economic growth.
key_facts: The China-Pakistan Free Trade Agreement (CPFTA) provides a framework for expanded bilateral trade.
Key sectors for export growth include agricultural products like rice, citrus fruits, and seafood.
Value addition in mineral resources like copper and granite is necessary for better market penetration.
The textile industry is urged to move toward finished goods like sportswear and home textiles rather than bulk fabric.

vocab.meaning: improving the economic value of ore by removing impurities
